transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

My mind keeps drifting off in meetings and calls, and I get distracted so easily that it’s starting to hurt my performance as a supervisor. I'm really struggling to stay mentally present when it matters most, and I need to figure out why this is happening.
Have you struggled with these focus and distraction issues since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently?

They've gotten much worse and really started disrupting my life since my promotion about 14 months ago, but the truth is this goes all the way back to my childhood. Even in elementary school, my report cards always said I daydreamed in class, forgot to turn in homework, and couldn't sit still without talking or fidgeting.
Along with these focus difficulties, have you also been experiencing a persistently down or sad mood, or a loss of interest in things you usually enjoy?

No, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or losing interest in things, even though I'm under a lot of stress right now with my divorce and the new job. I still really love playing my guitar and spending time with my son; my issue is more about staying focused and sitting still, rather than a lack of interest.
Do you find yourself experiencing constant, excessive worry about various everyday things—like your work, family, or future—that feels very difficult to control?

No, I wouldn't say I have constant, uncontrollable worry. I definitely feel stressed about my divorce and the mistakes I'm making at work, but it's more about feeling overwhelmed by my own disorganization and forgetfulness rather than generalized anxiety.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a classic history of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Type (F90.0). He describes prominent symptoms of inattention (distractibility, mind drifting, disorganization, forgetfulness) and childhood hyperactivity/impulsivity (fidgeting, inability to sit still, excessive talking) that have persisted from elementary school into adulthood. These symptoms are currently causing significant occupational impairment in his role as a supervisor. Alternative diagnoses such as Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) and Depressive Episode (F32.9) were considered but ruled out, as the patient denies persistent low mood, anhedonia, or generalized, uncontrollable worry, attributing his current stress directly to his ADHD-related difficulties and life stressors.
